> Threshold choice in relation to wear location and age group: I am guessing you are working with hip data, correct? If not, how did you arrive at this threshold? > Discrepancy with analytical approach by Actilife setting used. If you used Actilife to classify behaviour based on shorter epochs then I would expect that to result in more active time. If Actilife was used with some kind of bout or sojourn detection algorithm then I would expect it to result in lest active time.
> Mix-up of participant IDs. Double check that start date makes sense and is consistent between Actilife and GGIR. Ideally we never make these kind of mistakes, but can be good to double check.

Op woensdag 21 december 2022 om 04:35:35 UTC+10:30 schreef Vincent van Hees:
Dear Iris,

I see you chose a moderate threshold of 69 with a 1 minute epoch without considering consider bouts. The possible explanations that may be worth investigating:
Threshold choice in relation to wear location and age group: I am guessing you are working with hip data, correct? If not, how did you arrive at this threshold? If yes, then I suppose what you do is in line with literature for adult populations https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/GGIR/vignettes/CutPoints.html
Calibration of the data: Should not be a problem if you have several days of data with good compliance. See part2_summary variable calib_err, if this is below 0.005 then it should be good.
Choice of metric in relation to wear location. Metric ENMO has primarily been motivated for studies with wrist-worn sensors. It may be worth trying out the MAD metric (see cut-points Vähä-Ypyä 2015).
Discrepancy with analytical approach by Actilife setting used. If you used Actilife to classify behaviour based on shorter epochs then I would expect that to result in more active time. If Actilife was used with some kind of bout or sojourn detection algorithm then I would expect it to result in lest active time.
Mix-up of participant IDs. Double check that start date makes sense and is consistent between Actilife and GGIR. Ideally we never make these kind of mistakes, but can be good to double check.

Kind regards,

Vincent

Hi Bryan,

Sorry, I now see that our thread has been idle since December. I have been offline and now catching up.

Your rar file does not include the meta/basic folder content, by which I am not able to reproduce the error. However, I just had another look at your script and see "winhr = c(0.16667, 0.5, 1.0)". This would mean that you ask GGIR to look for the most active consecutive 10 minutes in the day.

If you are trying to replicate the MX metrics by Alex Rowlands and colleagues then please not that you should extract them with the qlevels argument in GGIR, which looks at the percentile corresponding to the most active non-consecutive X minutes or hours in a day.

I know it is very confusing that both methods can be referred to as MX, but there is a big difference in looking for the most active consecutive or non-consecutive minutes.

May I propose that you first try to process your data without specifying arguments winhr and qlevels (set them to c() or delete the config.csv file). Once that generates plausible output, refine your analyse by iteratively adding a new argument and running the analysis to identify whether and when you run into new error. For this new iterations you do not need to specify mode = 1 anymore, because there arguments will only affect part 2 analyses. However, I would recommend not using winhr with values less than 1 any longer as I am not sure there is any theoretical basis for it and because GGIR may not be ready to make sense of it either.

Best, Vincent

So, one solution for the future could be to slowly deprecate the old arguments and make threshold.mod work for both part 2 and 5, but obviously that would then have to come with clear warning to the user and good documentation to avoid any misunderstanding.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Cathy,

You are using rmc.check4timegaps =TRUE in the read.myacc.csv attempt and you do not use it in your GGIR() attempt. Please make sure the arguments are consistent.

Commenting arguments out with # does not reset them to default, they will only be reset to default if you delete the corresponding config.csv file in the output folder, because GGIR falls back on the config.csv file, if present, before falling back to the defaults inside the code.
Axivity devices had the problem that they started with a few seconds of zero's in the file. I am not sure, but possibly this can now be handled with rmc.check4timegaps =TRUE.
You will need to set rmc.doresample to TRUE because you exported the data without resampling, and GGIR wants a consistent sample rate throughout the recording.

Note that .cwa files are probably more compact to store than the compressed csv files, but I guess either way should be useful for research.

Regarding Jairo's comment - At some point I tried to facilitate Axivity csv format and it may still work, but I later  realised that OMGUI facilitates a lot of sub versions of csv format and it felt tricky to try to auto-detect all those variations. The read.myacc.csv route would seem more practical as you as a user will be in control of how the file is handled.

Best,

Vincent

To generate Mx acceleration values you need to specify the times in the qlevels function in part 2. Nathan Dawkins describes this in section 2.4.1 here: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33459582.

So, for the Mx metrics you have specified you would need qlevels = c(c(480/1440),c(1320/1440),c(1380/1440),c(1410/1440),c(1425/1440),c(1435/1440),c(1438/1440)),
where M2 = c(1438/1440) and so on. These are outputted into part2 as a percentage, so M2 column name will be "p99.86111_ENMO_mg_0.24hr" and that is the lowest acceleration value for the most active 2 minutes of the 24h day which we display on the radar plots. Hope that makes sense

On a side note, as it's not specified in Rowlands 2019, we made the code accessible through Github to generate the radar plots the same way that we did. The repository can be found here with a detailed breakdown of instructions:
https://github.com/Maylor8/RadarPlotGenerator.

Thanks,
Ben

Hello,

In regards to non-wear detection, I was wondering about the motivation behind the decision to label only the middle 15 minutes of the detected non-wear period and not the full 60-minute window that the 'non-wear test' was performed on?

I understand the importance of taking 15-minute steps, looking at 60-minute windows, but it seems to me that labelling the full 60-minute window would be more appropriate since the entire window is passing the non-wear test? Unless, there was some original design motivation that I am missing? Just wondering if Vincent or anyone had any insights on this and if it should be changed?

Thanks, Matt

messages.subject_clean: [GGIR] Non-wear time labelling
messages.body_plain:
Hi Matt,

Good point, and this is actually work in progress.
https://github.com/wadpac/GGIR/issues/645
https://github.com/wadpac/GGIR/pull/646

When I create the algorithm I was keen to make it conservative in its classifications of nonwear. My reasoning was that it is better to miss some nonwear here and there then to accidently mislabel large chunks of inactivity as nonwear. However, I later realised that this concern may not have been fully justified given that a signal with a variance close to noise for an hour must truly represent non-wear for that entire hour.

Last year Jairo also observed that there is room for improvement at the start and end of the labelled non-wear. He then proposed a revision to the algorithm in September, which worked well. However, after some discussion and reflection we came to the conclusion that the revision was too complex to describe in a paper and that labelling the entire 60 minute window as you also suggest possibly makes it easier to motivate the whole approach.

Obviously this new approach will break consistency at a fairly fundamental point in GGIR. So, it will be key for us to preserve the old (current) functionality as an option and to communicate clearly to users how the algorithm changed and how to choose the new or old approach.

Thanks,
Vincent
